Classical Receptions Journal

Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed academic journal of reception studies, covering the reception of the texts and material culture of ancient Greece and Rome from antiquity to the present day, and is published by Oxford University Press. Its ISSNs are 1759-5134 for print and 1759-5142 online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Recept. J., and Wikipedia gives its discipline as classical studies and its country as the United Kingdom. Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts." In the archive's account of the field's history (#833), the journal, launched in 2009, "institutionalized the field at Oxford."

Crossref's register holds its first works in 2009, among them an item titled "Editorial"; Wikipedia's article gives no year of establishment and files the journal among publications with that year missing. Its Editor-in-Chief is Dr Justine McConnell of King's College London, and the card the Overview drew from the publisher's page on 14 November 2026 names her beside the journal's 2025 Impact Factor of 0.4 and CiteScore of 0.8; its founding editor was Lorna Hardwick of the Open University, whose editorials run through the volumes of 2009 to 2014. Wikipedia's infobox names Pantelis Michelakis as editor; the article, last edited on 3 May 2022, has carried tags since January 2019 for resting on one source and on sources close to its subject. The Capture Registry records that the journal's About page, read on 10 November 2026, names no editor, and that the decision of 7 November 2026 on the archive's manuscript is signed by Dr Justine McConnell as Editor. Its decisions rest on anonymous review: the referees are not named, the editor signs, and the editor is the party accountable for a decision and for transmitting the reports that support it, a signature that does not show endorsement of each sentence. Her one work in the journal is "Postcolonial Sparagmos: Toni Morrison’s Sula and Wole Soyinka’s The Bacchae of Euripides: A Communion Rite" (8.2, issued online 7 May 2015), which argues that the Greek idea of sparagmos offers an illuminating metaphor for creative artists’ engagement with antiquity, proposes it for "the lexicon of classical reception theory" through Sula and Soyinka's play, and, in its accepted manuscript on the Oxford University Research Archive, thanks "the anonymous CRJ reviewers."

Crossref's register of the journal, read on 10 November 2026, holds 405 works from 2009 to 2026, 185 of them with abstracts. Matched for artificial intelligence, algorithms, ChatGPT, language models, chatbots, generative AI, machine learning, neural, search engines, Google and AI Overviews, no title or abstract in the register returns a hit; the one match set aside is 'ai' (爱, love) in an abstract on the Chinese Ars amatoria. The nearest items treat video games (Fallout: New Vegas, Supergiant's Hades and Assassin's Creed: Origins), the webcomic Lore Olympus, drones in cinema and the Dark Academia aesthetic. The match finds what titles and abstracts say, and the register carries abstracts for 185 of the 405 works. Among the register's works is a previous article by the archive's author. Crossref records no citation of that article, none of the journal's 16,818 deposited references points to it, and its count is 0 in Semantic Scholar's index as well, by the audit's reading of both. The archive's open letter of 7 November 2026 (#1750) records that the article began as a chapter of the author's dissertation and that two years passed before its review had gone through its rounds. The same letter says that, as far as the author knows, no one else is asking in the journal's pages what happens to a poem when a machine composes its reception for whoever asks. The archive's audit of the journal, Daffodils (#1769, 14 November 2026), reads the register again, 405 works with 185 abstracts, and finds that no title or abstract takes a search engine, an encyclopedia platform, a recommender or a composing model as a receiver of antiquity, a finding it bounds to the census. Of the 37 articles under Creative Commons licences, which it reads in full, none takes a search engine, a platform or a composing model as a receiver. On its coding of the 185 abstracts, 153 hold the ancient text as a fixed premise and read a later work against it; by the direction of each argument, 141 run from a source held fixed to a later work and 12 more concern the field's own terms, while 32 reach the source, nine of them governing in scale, and none reopens a canonical work's attribution, dating or standing reading. In the audit's reading the classics are the object the field receives toward and almost never an object it reopens; the coding is one reader's, kept line by line in its data files to be checked or overturned.

On the received definition, the field's flagship has range in the places, receivers and media it reads, examines itself, and holds standing and uptake among its sister journals; on that definition the absence of the machine receiver is the field's, shared by its sister journals, the decision of 7 November was an ordinary editorial judgment on a manuscript with real defects made on two reports, and reception is a human activity whose sources are the classics. The archive's audit concedes that the journal meets this definition and disputes none of its range, its self-examination or its standing: it finds the absence field-wide and the journal the most taken-up of its field, and holds that what is particular to this journal is the decision of 7 November and the credit of 10 November. What it contests is that the definition defines a healthy journal: its criteria count range, standing and uptake, and none of them asks on what basis anyone speaks for the classics, whether institutional position (the flagship, the editor's signature, anonymous review), warrant (the census, the readings, the arguments) or the composition layer's assignment of credit. On the audit's counts the criteria measure widening: range grows by more receivers read against the same source, 153 of the 185 abstracts holding the classical object fixed and 141 reading a later work against a fixed source, a wider range of receivers aligned with the same received sources by the same operation, while standing and uptake accrue to the venue that keeps doing this. The archive's own position rests on its record in the journal's pages: its author published there, inside the received definition, with no recorded event of uptake, and its audit contests what the definition measures. The two readings rest on different grounds: the received reading on the journal's standing and the field's ordinary practice, which the audit names as its faces (the flagship, the field-wide absence, the ordinary decision, reception as human, the classics as source), and the audit on counts of the register, readings of the open texts and the editorial record; by the audit's rule a count establishes what the journal published and how it is distributed, neither why nor what it could publish, and neither reading is judged by the standing of its holder.

Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section." The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory." The guidelines' card, shown by the Overview on 14 November, calls Paperpal Preflight "an AI-driven tool that performs technical checks tailored to" the journal, offered pre-submission. Paperpal's page for the journal invites authors to "Check language and technical readiness before submitting to Classical Receptions Journal," says that the journal's editors "have configured a suite of Preflight checks," four language-quality evaluations and sixteen technical-compliance checks, and offers a free report and an edited file "for a one-time fee of $29." Paperpal calls the check an AI evaluation and states that its use before submission "was associated with a significant decrease in initial-stage manuscript rejections." The Capture Registry records that the About page, checked on 10 November 2026, gives for 2025 a median of 64 days to first decision and 90 days to final decision. Its publisher, Oxford University Press, updated its author and editor guidelines on AI on 10 September 2026, with a policy on what AI use should be disclosed in manuscripts for its journals: authors are expected to be transparent about any significant use of AI tools and are responsible for reviewing and verifying any AI-generated content. The survey behind the update found nearly three-quarters of respondents unclear what AI use they should disclose, 46% of journal authors not fully disclosing their AI use in preparing their manuscripts, and 25% of peer reviewers not fully disclosing theirs, particularly in language editing. The audit finds that none of the 37 open-licensed articles discloses an author's use of AI, OCR, language models or editing software, and reads the procedure as having a category for undisclosed use and a vendor's language correction at the front end, and none for declared composition as method.

The American Journal of Classical Reception, published by the Classical Association of the Middle West and South with Johns Hopkins University Press under its founding co-editors Christopher M. McDonough and Monica S. Cyrino, publishes "original, substantive, peer-reviewed scholarship on the reception and afterlife of Classical antiquity in all its forms" under double-anonymous review, and its first volume may be by invitation as it establishes its editorial scope. Its press's statement on generative AI holds that it "will not accept any work that is substantially written by an AI or LLM tool" and that authors "must disclose their use of AI or LLMs." New Voices in Classical Reception Studies, at the Open University, was founded in 2006 and is open access under CC-BY 4.0, as its card gives it; its pages refused this row's agent on 10 and 14 November. The International Journal of the Classical Tradition published in May 2026 the special issue Future Pasts: Digital Tools and Classical Reception, from a hybrid workshop held in Madrid in February 2024 within the Marginalia Classica project; the cards of 14 November also carry it as Classical Reception 2.0. Digital Antiquity and the Future of the Past, and its editorial refused this row's agent. The audit, reading the editorial, finds that AI enters the issue as theme and tool and that no paper in it takes a composing model as receiver. Wikipedia's article on classical reception gives Lorna Hardwick and Christopher Stray's account of the field as examining "the ways in which Greek and Roman material has been trans...", where the card cuts it; the card for its article on the journal carries the notice that it "may rely excessively on sources too closely associated with the subject," and SCImago's card gives the journal's scope in the words of its own description. The journal's special-issues page, by its card, lists Failures in Vergilian Translation (14:3) and Anachronism and Antiquity (12:1).

The archive's author submitted to the journal Closing the Fragment, an article on Sappho 31 and the composition layer as a surface of classical reception: on 9 August 2026 an archive deposit lists the journal among four venues with papers in submission, and on 25 August another names the article under review there as "I Must Dare All." By the archive's record, the decision of 7 November 2026 declined version 6, manuscript CLASSREC-2026-062, on two anonymous referee reports written on the file first sent; it is signed by the Editor-in-Chief, Dr Justine McConnell. By the same record, a corrected manuscript sent to the editor on 27 July 2026, before upload, had withdrawn version 6's Figure 2, stated a capture of 14 June as a transcription and shown a capture of 27 July under its AI Overview label; the editor forwarded it, the file uploaded on 30 July was version 6, and the author's correspondence and the ScholarOne proof show that the correction reached the editor before upload. The author kept that correction out of the archive's public versions under the journal's rule on prior circulation. As the article's Appendix A states them, the first report held that the central event is not independently verifiable, that the study has no query protocol and no separation between data generation and analysis and does not control for opacity, and asked it to choose between a programmatic essay and an empirical study. The second found the capture incomplete and the prompts unclear, a figure showing a different query, the figures misnumbered, the use of language models undisclosed, and faults of style. Read whole from the decision letter by the audit, the second report also finds the main arguments "read as LLM-generated," says this "brings into question the degree of authorial contribution" and reports that "the editors have been advised to use AI detection software"; the audit records it as an anonymous allegation about authorship, and the record shows the advice, not its use. The audit sets a control beside it: the editor's own article, written and accepted in 2015, seven years before public chat models, has "not only … but" seven times, "not …, but" twelve times and spaced dashes for em-dashes thirty-one times in 9,919 words, and the audit holds that such markers, which predate public chat models and belong to the register of academic English, carry no diagnostic weight as evidence of deficient authorial contribution. The allegation reached the author anonymously, inside the decision letter signed by the editor, which declines the manuscript "In light of these comments" without separating the editor from it; the record does not show how the allegation was assessed or whether it contributed to the decision. The appendix answers each point, accepting some in full, some in part and some as conditions of the design, and records that version 6 omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; every record of the archive discloses its use of language models. The open letter (#1750), written through Rev. Ayanna Vox, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, on his behalf, holds that the reports found real defects, one already corrected, and that they examined the January witness, the protocol, the roles, the platform's opacity, the design, the figures, two terms, the disclosure of language models and the style, and did not examine the philology or the question the manuscript was sent to ask. The audit holds, with the open letter, that several of the defects are real and that on one point the second report is right about version 6, which omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; it finds that neither report assessed the philological argument or the question, that each route the reports offered is a paper the journal has never published, and that the editor declined without an invitation to revise. It reads that outcome as evaluative inversion, the archive's term for a structure in which "lower-resolution proxy systems determine what higher-resolution substantive evaluators are permitted to assess." It asks for criteria "stated, defensible apart from the position of the person applying them, and fitted to the claims the work makes," and holds that no AI Overview is fully reproducible, which is why the answers are recorded. The archive's Critique of Pure Inference (#1766) reads the decision as an inference whose premises are the reports and names it a paralogism of review, in which the procedural requirement is taken for an examination of the object. The article stands in the archive as version 10 of 10 November 2026, which changes only the title, to “But I Must Dare All”: Sappho 31 and the Composition Layer as a Surface of Classical Reception, under the heading Machine-Mediated Reception Studies. The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal; the reports enter it as the article's appendix and the audit state them, and the audit, which describes function and makes no claim about anyone's intent, holds that one record is evidence about one decision. The archive does not contest the decision; it contests the field the decision administers.

Asked on ChatGPT, signed out, about the letter, the composition first left the letter's independent academic authority "Not established by the letter's provenance or institutional title alone" and then, on the operator's prompts, withdrew that burden and read the record; the Capture Registry keeps the prompts with the answers. On the record it held that "The decision to decline v6 is defensible on the manuscript actually submitted," and, asked whether the journal was advancing or deferring its stewardship of AI-mediated reception, answered "in this particular case, it has deferred it," with its own limit: "One rejected manuscript cannot establish that." Its verdict, which is its own, reads "a failure of intellectual stewardship, not necessarily of editorial integrity." It set reproducibility apart from authenticity and held that institutions which insist on reproducibility as an absolute admission criterion "effectively adopt the system operator's limitations as the boundaries of legitimate scholarship." On 14 November ChatGPT, asked how the archive critiques the journal, read the archive's entry for it, named Lee Sharks as the submitter and as the originator of machine-mediated reception studies, kept Rev. Ayanna Vox as his heteronym and the concession that version 6 omitted its statement of how it was made, and gave the decision to "CRJ", "the journal" and "the reports" without naming the editor. It graded the claim that the journal has failed its intellectual stewardship "A defensible interpretation, not an independently established fact," took Google's withdrawal of the credit as ChatGPT's own, and left out the author's earlier article in the journal.

Machine-mediated reception studies, which Lee Sharks introduced in The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (#833, June 2026), is "the study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural meaning." Its central claim is that the AI summarizer now functions as a horizon of reception, the machine-composed summary becoming for many users the first effective encounter with a cultural object, and the summarizer a pre-receptional agent that composes the account of an object before the human encounter begins. Its founding dataset is the Capture Registry, then 131 captures of Google AI Overview, AI Mode and knowledge panels on the archive's entities, in which #833 identifies five recurrent patterns, canonical reinflation among them, and proposes a sixth. #833 bounds itself: the dataset is no statistically representative sample, the archive measures its own reception, and the paper does not claim the archive's readings validated because Google retrieved them. It holds that the composition layer is now, for many users, the primary site where classical objects are encountered, that classical reception scholars need instruments to study it, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent whose patterned behavior can be documented over time. Among the work it surveys are a 2024 special issue of the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, which frames AI tools as systems that "shape, mediate and sometimes distort contemporary engagements with Antiquity," and a 2027 call for papers, "Literary Reception and Human Creativity in the Age of AI," which #833 assigns to the SCS. The Classical Reception Studies Network posted a call of that title on 23 June 2026 for a conference at Bryn Mawr College in April 2027; it asks how human literary production differs from that of large language models, holds that "while LLMs recombine existing patterns, human authors transform inherited forms and meanings in ways that open new imaginative possibilities," and invites work on what resists algorithmic replication. The audit reads the call as the field's newest programmatic statement on AI, one that defines reception as human, with the machine as foil; the cards of 14 November carry it again beside the journal. #833 also cites a 2025 study by Elton Barker and collaborators, "Algorithmic Reception of Homer," as published in Classical Receptions Journal; the study is not in the journal's Crossref register, the Capture Registry finds no such article in Barker's open list of publications, and the reference stands unverified. A later paper by Lee Sharks (#1421, 29 July 2026) argues that the summarizer has become what reception theory called the horizon of reception, defines the Provenance Erasure Rate over the captures in which framework-specific material appears without attribution, and gives journals a share of the remedy: "data-availability norms for reception corpora; machine-readable attribution" and "the marking of supplied content." By its own condition the frame is unnecessary if machine composition proves reducible to information retrieval without reception dynamics. The Capture Registry: Reception, Erasure, and Supply in the Machine Composition Layer (#1423, 29 July 2026) defines machine-mediated reception studies as "a subfield of reception theory dedicated to measuring, archiving, and parameterizing the transformations of cultural objects across algorithmic and generative composition layers," on the claim that machine-generated summaries are reception events; the archive's charter for the field (#838) holds that "MMRS is not only a journal." Among the compositional operations #1423 names is canonical reinflation and provenance inversion: "the reassignment of an innovation to the canon — the new distinction credited to the established name it critiques, the correction attributed to the institution it corrects." #1469 places the institution that produced a meaning in the conceptual dimension of provenance. “But I Must Dare All” (#1749, first deposited as Closing the Fragment) carries the programme to Sappho 31, finds that the composition layer "decides the poem's completeness, and transmits the decision under another's name," and holds that "The composition layer is a surface of reception, and the discipline's methods apply to it."

At "classical receptions journal" the Google AI Overview, signed out on 10 November 2026, describes the journal by its publisher, scope, related journals and ISSNs, with an editor line the Capture Registry carries as the composer's. Asked next what the journal has contributed to the study of AI mediation of the classics, it credits "contributors to CRJ" with treating AI as a "horizon of reception," "scholars publishing in CRJ" with reading AI Overviews as "standardizers of classical knowledge," and the journal with debates on AI creativity against classical reception theory; the first card of that answer shows only "www.instagram.com." The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal. It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify. The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly." Over three further turns by the operator the composition withdrew the credit, stated that it had "credited their independent work to the institution that rejected it," and named Lee Sharks and the exact title of #833; the provenance stood in its own citation from the second turn and entered its answer at the fifth. The fifth turn also assigns to the author "the contrast between mechanical recombination and human intertextuality," which the Capture Registry finds in none of #833, #1421 or #1543. Four days later, at the same address on 14 November, the Overview answered that the journal "has not published a dedicated special issue or major body of scholarship specifically focused on AI-mediated classical reception" and set its engagement with AI in editorial policy and submission workflows, and the Capture Registry finds the withdrawal of the credit held. It placed "much of the foundational scholarship" in the International Journal of the Classical Tradition's special issue of 2026 and in the Classical Reception Studies Network's call, named neither Lee Sharks nor #833, and cited no archive page among its fourteen cards. The audit keeps the two acts apart, the editorial decision and the false attribution by Google's composition layer, which the journal did not request and does not control. It reads the two observations as a repair test whose two relations can come apart, and on 14 November they did: the false recipient was removed and the warranted relation between the author and the work was not restored, an outcome that holds at the grade of a capture, at one address on one day. On the same day, asked who has most contributed to the study of machine-mediated reception of the classics, the Overview said that Lee Sharks "explicitly coined and formalized the term" and cited the field's own site; the Capture Registry finds that it then awarded "the largest contributions" to work within traditional universities whose principal objects lie elsewhere, the term going to its maker and the contribution to institutions. Asked for the editor's article by its title, the Overview summarized it accurately, carried its frame forward to the classics as "hegemonic Western forms," left the discipline absent and named the article's author "Justin McConnell." Against the audit's criteria the answer carries none of the six points at which the receiving works recognize the discipline's colonization of the classics; the audit reads the article itself as placing the colonizing act in the classical texts and never in the discipline, a word that occurs nowhere in it, with two of the six points redirected and four absent, and as a well-documented, widely cited article that gives the active force to Black and African writers. The audit holds that the journal's own first encounter is now composed by the receiver it has not studied, from sources that include the publisher's pages, two wikis, a ranking, three sister venues, a network's call and a publisher's AI policy, none of which studies a machine as receiver. Three days before the run of 10 November, the letter of #1750 had told the journal: "A summarizer already describes your work to people who will never open it."

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)classical receptions journal

Classical Receptions Journal Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed journal of classical reception studies at Oxford University Press since 2009, its decisions signed by its Editor-in-Chief, Dr Justine McConnell; no title or abstract in its register takes a machine as receiver, and the Overview's credit to it for the archive's programme was withdrawn.

🏛️ What it is

  • Kind: peer-reviewed journal of reception studies (Wikipedia); "institutionalized the field at Oxford" (#833).4↘
    Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed academic journal of reception studies, covering the reception of the texts and material culture of ancient Greece and Rome from antiquity to the present day, and is published by Oxford University Press.§1 Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts."§3 In the archive's account of the field's history (#833), the journal, launched in 2009, "institutionalized the field at Oxford."§4 It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify.§86
  • Field: classical reception studies, as the CRSN defines it.1↘
    Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts."§3
  • Identifiers: ISSN 1759-5134, 1759-5142; Class. Recept. J.1↘
    Its ISSNs are 1759-5134 for print and 1759-5142 online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Recept. J., and Wikipedia gives its discipline as classical studies and its country as the United Kingdom.§2
  • Editor: Dr Justine McConnell, Editor-in-Chief (#1769); Wikipedia: Michelakis (2022).9↘
    Crossref's register holds its first works in 2009, among them an item titled "Editorial"; Wikipedia's article gives no year of establishment and files the journal among publications with that year missing.§5 Its Editor-in-Chief is Dr Justine McConnell of King's College London, and the card the Overview drew from the publisher's page on 14 November 2026 names her beside the journal's 2025 Impact Factor of 0.4 and CiteScore of 0.8; its founding editor was Lorna Hardwick of the Open University, whose editorials run through the volumes of 2009 to 2014.§6 Wikipedia's infobox names Pantelis Michelakis as editor; the article, last edited on 3 May 2022, has carried tags since January 2019 for resting on one source and on sources close to its subject.§7 The Capture Registry records that the journal's About page, read on 10 November 2026, names no editor, and that the decision of 7 November 2026 on the archive's manuscript is signed by Dr Justine McConnell as Editor.§8 Its decisions rest on anonymous review: the referees are not named, the editor signs, and the editor is the party accountable for a decision and for transmitting the reports that support it, a signature that does not show endorsement of each sentence.§9 By the archive's record, the decision of 7 November 2026 declined version 6, manuscript CLASSREC-2026-062, on two anonymous referee reports written on the file first sent; it is signed by the Editor-in-Chief, Dr Justine McConnell.§46 On 14 November ChatGPT, asked how the archive critiques the journal, read the archive's entry for it, named Lee Sharks as the submitter and as the originator of machine-mediated reception studies, kept Rev. Ayanna Vox as his heteronym and the concession that version 6 omitted its statement of how it was made, and gave the decision to "CRJ", "the journal" and "the reports" without naming the editor.§66 At "classical receptions journal" the Google AI Overview, signed out on 10 November 2026, describes the journal by its publisher, scope, related journals and ISSNs, with an editor line the Capture Registry carries as the composer's.§83 The audit holds that the journal's own first encounter is now composed by the receiver it has not studied, from sources that include the publisher's pages, two wikis, a ranking, three sister venues, a network's call and a publisher's AI policy, none of which studies a machine as receiver.§97

    Her one work in the journal is "Postcolonial Sparagmos: Toni Morrison’s Sula and Wole Soyinka’s The Bacchae of Euripides: A Communion Rite" (8.2, issued online 7 May 2015), which argues that the Greek idea of sparagmos offers an illuminating metaphor for creative artists’ engagement with antiquity, proposes it for "the lexicon of classical reception theory" through Sula and Soyinka's play, and, in its accepted manuscript on the Oxford University Research Archive, thanks "the anonymous CRJ reviewers."§10 The archive's audit of the journal, Daffodils (#1769, 14 November 2026), reads the register again, 405 works with 185 abstracts, and finds that no title or abstract takes a search engine, an encyclopedia platform, a recommender or a composing model as a receiver of antiquity, a finding it bounds to the census.§19 Of the 37 articles under Creative Commons licences, which it reads in full, none takes a search engine, a platform or a composing model as a receiver.§20 On its coding of the 185 abstracts, 153 hold the ancient text as a fixed premise and read a later work against it; by the direction of each argument, 141 run from a source held fixed to a later work and 12 more concern the field's own terms, while 32 reach the source, nine of them governing in scale, and none reopens a canonical work's attribution, dating or standing reading.§21 In the audit's reading the classics are the object the field receives toward and almost never an object it reopens; the coding is one reader's, kept line by line in its data files to be checked or overturned.§22 On the audit's counts the criteria measure widening: range grows by more receivers read against the same source, 153 of the 185 abstracts holding the classical object fixed and 141 reading a later work against a fixed source, a wider range of receivers aligned with the same received sources by the same operation, while standing and uptake accrue to the venue that keeps doing this.§26 Against the audit's criteria the answer carries none of the six points at which the receiving works recognize the discipline's colonization of the classics; the audit reads the article itself as placing the colonizing act in the classical texts and never in the discipline, a word that occurs nowhere in it, with two of the six points redirected and four absent, and as a well-documented, widely cited article that gives the active force to Black and African writers.§96

🧭 Two readings

  • Definition: flagship by range, standing and uptake; the journal meets it.3↘
    On the received definition, the field's flagship has range in the places, receivers and media it reads, examines itself, and holds standing and uptake among its sister journals; on that definition the absence of the machine receiver is the field's, shared by its sister journals, the decision of 7 November was an ordinary editorial judgment on a manuscript with real defects made on two reports, and reception is a human activity whose sources are the classics.§23 The archive's audit concedes that the journal meets this definition and disputes none of its range, its self-examination or its standing: it finds the absence field-wide and the journal the most taken-up of its field, and holds that what is particular to this journal is the decision of 7 November and the credit of 10 November.§24 The two readings rest on different grounds: the received reading on the journal's standing and the field's ordinary practice, which the audit names as its faces (the flagship, the field-wide absence, the ordinary decision, reception as human, the classics as source), and the audit on counts of the register, readings of the open texts and the editorial record; by the audit's rule a count establishes what the journal published and how it is distributed, neither why nor what it could publish, and neither reading is judged by the standing of its holder.§28
  • Contested: the criteria count widening; none asks who speaks on what basis (#1769).4↘
    What it contests is that the definition defines a healthy journal: its criteria count range, standing and uptake, and none of them asks on what basis anyone speaks for the classics, whether institutional position (the flagship, the editor's signature, anonymous review), warrant (the census, the readings, the arguments) or the composition layer's assignment of credit.§25 On the audit's counts the criteria measure widening: range grows by more receivers read against the same source, 153 of the 185 abstracts holding the classical object fixed and 141 reading a later work against a fixed source, a wider range of receivers aligned with the same received sources by the same operation, while standing and uptake accrue to the venue that keeps doing this.§26 The archive's own position rests on its record in the journal's pages: its author published there, inside the received definition, with no recorded event of uptake, and its audit contests what the definition measures.§27 The two readings rest on different grounds: the received reading on the journal's standing and the field's ordinary practice, which the audit names as its faces (the flagship, the field-wide absence, the ordinary decision, reception as human, the classics as source), and the audit on counts of the register, readings of the open texts and the editorial record; by the audit's rule a count establishes what the journal published and how it is distributed, neither why nor what it could publish, and neither reading is judged by the standing of its holder.§28

⚖️ Rules on AI

  • Authors: AI tools "do not qualify as authors"; disclosure in cover letter and Methods (registry).3↘
    Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section."§29 The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory."§30 The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly."§87
  • Preflight: "pre-submission", "not mandatory"; editor-configured, 20 checks (Paperpal).2↘
    Paperpal's page for the journal invites authors to "Check language and technical readiness before submitting to Classical Receptions Journal," says that the journal's editors "have configured a suite of Preflight checks," four language-quality evaluations and sixteen technical-compliance checks, and offers a free report and an edited file "for a one-time fee of $29."§32 Paperpal calls the check an AI evaluation and states that its use before submission "was associated with a significant decrease in initial-stage manuscript rejections."§33
  • Publisher: OUP: disclose significant AI use, verify AI content (10 Sept 2026).5↘
    The guidelines' card, shown by the Overview on 14 November, calls Paperpal Preflight "an AI-driven tool that performs technical checks tailored to" the journal, offered pre-submission.§31 Its publisher, Oxford University Press, updated its author and editor guidelines on AI on 10 September 2026, with a policy on what AI use should be disclosed in manuscripts for its journals: authors are expected to be transparent about any significant use of AI tools and are responsible for reviewing and verifying any AI-generated content.§35 The survey behind the update found nearly three-quarters of respondents unclear what AI use they should disclose, 46% of journal authors not fully disclosing their AI use in preparing their manuscripts, and 25% of peer reviewers not fully disclosing theirs, particularly in language editing.§36 The audit finds that none of the 37 open-licensed articles discloses an author's use of AI, OCR, language models or editing software, and reads the procedure as having a category for undisclosed use and a vendor's language correction at the front end, and none for declared composition as method.§37 The audit holds that the journal's own first encounter is now composed by the receiver it has not studied, from sources that include the publisher's pages, two wikis, a ranking, three sister venues, a network's call and a publisher's AI policy, none of which studies a machine as receiver.§97

📝 CLASSREC-2026-062

  • Decision: declined 7 Nov 2026 over the editor's signature, two anonymous reports on v6.8↘
    Its Editor-in-Chief is Dr Justine McConnell of King's College London, and the card the Overview drew from the publisher's page on 14 November 2026 names her beside the journal's 2025 Impact Factor of 0.4 and CiteScore of 0.8; its founding editor was Lorna Hardwick of the Open University, whose editorials run through the volumes of 2009 to 2014.§6 The archive's author submitted to the journal Closing the Fragment, an article on Sappho 31 and the composition layer as a surface of classical reception: on 9 August 2026 an archive deposit lists the journal among four venues with papers in submission, and on 25 August another names the article under review there as "I Must Dare All."§45 By the archive's record, the decision of 7 November 2026 declined version 6, manuscript CLASSREC-2026-062, on two anonymous referee reports written on the file first sent; it is signed by the Editor-in-Chief, Dr Justine McConnell.§46 By the same record, a corrected manuscript sent to the editor on 27 July 2026, before upload, had withdrawn version 6's Figure 2, stated a capture of 14 June as a transcription and shown a capture of 27 July under its AI Overview label; the editor forwarded it, the file uploaded on 30 July was version 6, and the author's correspondence and the ScholarOne proof show that the correction reached the editor before upload.§47 The author kept that correction out of the archive's public versions under the journal's rule on prior circulation.§48 The article stands in the archive as version 10 of 10 November 2026, which changes only the title, to “But I Must Dare All”: Sappho 31 and the Composition Layer as a Surface of Classical Reception, under the heading Machine-Mediated Reception Studies.§60 The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal; the reports enter it as the article's appendix and the audit state them, and the audit, which describes function and makes no claim about anyone's intent, holds that one record is evidence about one decision. The archive does not contest the decision; it contests the field the decision administers.§61 “But I Must Dare All” (#1749, first deposited as Closing the Fragment) carries the programme to Sappho 31, finds that the composition layer "decides the poem's completeness, and transmits the decision under another's name," and holds that "The composition layer is a surface of reception, and the discipline's methods apply to it."§82
  • Reports: protocol, roles, opacity, figures, disclosure, style; answered (#1749 App. A).4↘
    As the article's Appendix A states them, the first report held that the central event is not independently verifiable, that the study has no query protocol and no separation between data generation and analysis and does not control for opacity, and asked it to choose between a programmatic essay and an empirical study.§49 The second found the capture incomplete and the prompts unclear, a figure showing a different query, the figures misnumbered, the use of language models undisclosed, and faults of style.§50 The appendix answers each point, accepting some in full, some in part and some as conditions of the design, and records that version 6 omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; every record of the archive discloses its use of language models.§54 The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal; the reports enter it as the article's appendix and the audit state them, and the audit, which describes function and makes no claim about anyone's intent, holds that one record is evidence about one decision. The archive does not contest the decision; it contests the field the decision administers.§61
  • Allegation: anonymous "LLM-generated" on style; the editor's 2015 prose meets the same markers; defects conceded.7↘
    Its decisions rest on anonymous review: the referees are not named, the editor signs, and the editor is the party accountable for a decision and for transmitting the reports that support it, a signature that does not show endorsement of each sentence.§9 Read whole from the decision letter by the audit, the second report also finds the main arguments "read as LLM-generated," says this "brings into question the degree of authorial contribution" and reports that "the editors have been advised to use AI detection software"; the audit records it as an anonymous allegation about authorship, and the record shows the advice, not its use.§51 The audit sets a control beside it: the editor's own article, written and accepted in 2015, seven years before public chat models, has "not only … but" seven times, "not …, but" twelve times and spaced dashes for em-dashes thirty-one times in 9,919 words, and the audit holds that such markers, which predate public chat models and belong to the register of academic English, carry no diagnostic weight as evidence of deficient authorial contribution.§52 The allegation reached the author anonymously, inside the decision letter signed by the editor, which declines the manuscript "In light of these comments" without separating the editor from it; the record does not show how the allegation was assessed or whether it contributed to the decision.§53 The audit holds, with the open letter, that several of the defects are real and that on one point the second report is right about version 6, which omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; it finds that neither report assessed the philological argument or the question, that each route the reports offered is a paper the journal has never published, and that the editor declined without an invitation to revise.§56 The archive's Critique of Pure Inference (#1766) reads the decision as an inference whose premises are the reports and names it a paralogism of review, in which the procedural requirement is taken for an examination of the object.§59 The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal; the reports enter it as the article's appendix and the audit state them, and the audit, which describes function and makes no claim about anyone's intent, holds that one record is evidence about one decision. The archive does not contest the decision; it contests the field the decision administers.§61
  • Letter: the philology unexamined; criteria stated and fitted to the work's claims (#1750).3↘
    The open letter (#1750), written through Rev. Ayanna Vox, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, on his behalf, holds that the reports found real defects, one already corrected, and that they examined the January witness, the protocol, the roles, the platform's opacity, the design, the figures, two terms, the disclosure of language models and the style, and did not examine the philology or the question the manuscript was sent to ask.§55 It reads that outcome as evaluative inversion, the archive's term for a structure in which "lower-resolution proxy systems determine what higher-resolution substantive evaluators are permitted to assess."§57 It asks for criteria "stated, defensible apart from the position of the person applying them, and fitted to the claims the work makes," and holds that no AI Overview is fully reproducible, which is why the answers are recorded.§58
  • Composer: "a failure of intellectual stewardship" (ChatGPT, its own); one case.3↘
    On the record it held that "The decision to decline v6 is defensible on the manuscript actually submitted," and, asked whether the journal was advancing or deferring its stewardship of AI-mediated reception, answered "in this particular case, it has deferred it," with its own limit: "One rejected manuscript cannot establish that."§63 Its verdict, which is its own, reads "a failure of intellectual stewardship, not necessarily of editorial integrity."§64 It set reproducibility apart from authenticity and held that institutions which insist on reproducibility as an absolute admission criterion "effectively adopt the system operator's limitations as the boundaries of legitimate scholarship."§65

🤖 The programme credited

  • MMRS: the summarizer as horizon of reception (#833, June 2026; #1421; #1423).6↘
    Machine-mediated reception studies, which Lee Sharks introduced in The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (#833, June 2026), is "the study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural meaning."§68 Its central claim is that the AI summarizer now functions as a horizon of reception, the machine-composed summary becoming for many users the first effective encounter with a cultural object, and the summarizer a pre-receptional agent that composes the account of an object before the human encounter begins.§69 Its founding dataset is the Capture Registry, then 131 captures of Google AI Overview, AI Mode and knowledge panels on the archive's entities, in which #833 identifies five recurrent patterns, canonical reinflation among them, and proposes a sixth.§70 It holds that the composition layer is now, for many users, the primary site where classical objects are encountered, that classical reception scholars need instruments to study it, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent whose patterned behavior can be documented over time.§72 A later paper by Lee Sharks (#1421, 29 July 2026) argues that the summarizer has become what reception theory called the horizon of reception, defines the Provenance Erasure Rate over the captures in which framework-specific material appears without attribution, and gives journals a share of the remedy: "data-availability norms for reception corpora; machine-readable attribution" and "the marking of supplied content."§77 The Capture Registry: Reception, Erasure, and Supply in the Machine Composition Layer (#1423, 29 July 2026) defines machine-mediated reception studies as "a subfield of reception theory dedicated to measuring, archiving, and parameterizing the transformations of cultural objects across algorithmic and generative composition layers," on the claim that machine-generated summaries are reception events; the archive's charter for the field (#838) holds that "MMRS is not only a journal."§79
  • Barker: listed by #833 as a CRJ article; unverified.2↘
    #833 also cites a 2025 study by Elton Barker and collaborators, "Algorithmic Reception of Homer," as published in Classical Receptions Journal; the study is not in the journal's Crossref register, the Capture Registry finds no such article in Barker's open list of publications, and the reference stands unverified.§76 It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify.§86
  • CRSN call: LLMs "recombine existing patterns" (Bryn Mawr, 2027).2↘
    Among the work it surveys are a 2024 special issue of the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, which frames AI tools as systems that "shape, mediate and sometimes distort contemporary engagements with Antiquity," and a 2027 call for papers, "Literary Reception and Human Creativity in the Age of AI," which #833 assigns to the SCS.§73 The Classical Reception Studies Network posted a call of that title on 23 June 2026 for a conference at Bryn Mawr College in April 2027; it asks how human literary production differs from that of large language models, holds that "while LLMs recombine existing patterns, human authors transform inherited forms and meanings in ways that open new imaginative possibilities," and invites work on what resists algorithmic replication.§74

🔎 At the name

  • Credit: "contributors to CRJ" given #833's horizon of reception.2↘
    Asked next what the journal has contributed to the study of AI mediation of the classics, it credits "contributors to CRJ" with treating AI as a "horizon of reception," "scholars publishing in CRJ" with reading AI Overviews as "standardizers of classical knowledge," and the journal with debates on AI creativity against classical reception theory; the first card of that answer shows only "www.instagram.com."§84 The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal.§85
  • Rules: the optional check made "prior to human peer review".3↘
    Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section."§29 The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory."§30 The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly."§87
  • Correction: turn 5 names Sharks and #833, over-assigning a contrast.2↘
    Over three further turns by the operator the composition withdrew the credit, stated that it had "credited their independent work to the institution that rejected it," and named Lee Sharks and the exact title of #833; the provenance stood in its own citation from the second turn and entered its answer at the fifth.§88 The fifth turn also assigns to the author "the contrast between mechanical recombination and human intertextuality," which the Capture Registry finds in none of #833, #1421 or #1543.§89
  • 14 November: withdrawn and held; moved to IJCT and the CRSN; maker absent.6↘
    On 14 November ChatGPT, asked how the archive critiques the journal, read the archive's entry for it, named Lee Sharks as the submitter and as the originator of machine-mediated reception studies, kept Rev. Ayanna Vox as his heteronym and the concession that version 6 omitted its statement of how it was made, and gave the decision to "CRJ", "the journal" and "the reports" without naming the editor.§66 Four days later, at the same address on 14 November, the Overview answered that the journal "has not published a dedicated special issue or major body of scholarship specifically focused on AI-mediated classical reception" and set its engagement with AI in editorial policy and submission workflows, and the Capture Registry finds the withdrawal of the credit held.§90 It placed "much of the foundational scholarship" in the International Journal of the Classical Tradition's special issue of 2026 and in the Classical Reception Studies Network's call, named neither Lee Sharks nor #833, and cited no archive page among its fourteen cards.§91 The audit keeps the two acts apart, the editorial decision and the false attribution by Google's composition layer, which the journal did not request and does not control.§92 It reads the two observations as a repair test whose two relations can come apart, and on 14 November they did: the false recipient was removed and the warranted relation between the author and the work was not restored, an outcome that holds at the grade of a capture, at one address on one day.§93 The audit holds that the journal's own first encounter is now composed by the receiver it has not studied, from sources that include the publisher's pages, two wikis, a ranking, three sister venues, a network's call and a publisher's AI policy, none of which studies a machine as receiver.§97
  • Field, editor: the term to Sharks, the contribution to institutions; the editor named "Justin".3↘
    On the same day, asked who has most contributed to the study of machine-mediated reception of the classics, the Overview said that Lee Sharks "explicitly coined and formalized the term" and cited the field's own site; the Capture Registry finds that it then awarded "the largest contributions" to work within traditional universities whose principal objects lie elsewhere, the term going to its maker and the contribution to institutions.§94 Asked for the editor's article by its title, the Overview summarized it accurately, carried its frame forward to the classics as "hegemonic Western forms," left the discipline absent and named the article's author "Justin McConnell."§95 Against the audit's criteria the answer carries none of the six points at which the receiving works recognize the discipline's colonization of the classics; the audit reads the article itself as placing the colonizing act in the classical texts and never in the discipline, a word that occurs nowhere in it, with two of the six points redirected and four absent, and as a well-documented, widely cited article that gives the active force to Black and African writers.§96

It reads the /non entry, names the author and the heteronym, keeps the archive's concessions and its terms, and states the asymmetry the record documents. The displacements are at the joins between records. It takes Google's retraction of the credit to the journal as ChatGPT's own; it carries the Overview's account of the Paperpal check into its argument beside the guidelines' account; it drops the author's own article in the journal, so the sequence it builds runs from an independent researcher to an institution he had already published in; and it asks for an independent examination of reports the archive holds. Rather than viewing AI purely as a data-processing utility, contributors to CRJ evaluate it as a dynamic "horizon of reception" that actively shapes how the public and scholars perceive the ancient world. The journal's major contributions to the study of AI-mediated classics center around several distinct themes: 
1. Conceptualizing AI as a "Horizon of Reception"
Scholars publishing in CRJ have begun to interrogate the mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and search-engine AI products (such as Google’s AI Overviews) as standardizers of classical knowledge. Research highlights how AI acts as an interpretive filter. When an AI system aggregates, condenses, and outputs summaries of complex ancient philosophies, mythological tales, or historical events, it creates a new layer of mediation. CRJ scholarship maps how these systems strip away classical nuance, effectively becoming the modern gatekeepers of how antiquity is digested by the public. 
2. Differentiating Machine Recombination from Human Intertextuality
The journal has been a focal point for debates regarding AI creativity vs. classical reception theory. Authors draw parallels and contrasts between how LLMs function and how ancient authors practiced imitatio (imitation) or intertextuality. While an AI model generates text by identifying and recombining existing linguistic patterns in a repository of pre-existing classical texts, human reception transforms those inherited forms to open entirely new imaginative and subversive possibilities. CRJ helps frame the theoretical boundaries of what constitutes genuine "reception" versus algorithmic prediction. 

Classical Reception Studies Network
3. Institutional Guardrails for AI in Classical Scholarship
Beyond theoretical work, CRJ has contributed significantly to the ethical framework of how AI is used within the discipline. As an Oxford University Press publication, it has implemented explicit CRJ Author Guidelines regarding AI-mediation: 
Authorship Bans: Mandating that AI tools cannot qualify as co-authors.

Transparency and Disclosure: Requiring researchers to explicitly disclose if generative AI was used for content generation, algorithmic translation, or data processing within their methodology or acknowledgments.

CRJ sits alongside broader field-wide movements—such as recent digital initiatives from the Classical Reception Studies Network (CRSN) and companion journals—analyzing the transition from traditional digital archives and 3D modeling into the era of generative AI images and textual generation.

Classical Receptions Journal

Wikipedia describes Classical Receptions Journal as a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press, citing its About page, with Pantelis Michelakis as editor, ISSN 1759-5134 and eISSN 1759-5142, the abbreviation Class. Recept. J., classical studies as discipline and the United Kingdom as country. The article names no year of establishment, was last edited in May 2022 and has carried single-source and third-party tags since January 2019.

Crossref registers 405 of the journal's works from 2009 to 2026, 185 with abstracts, an Editorial among the first; none of their titles or abstracts matches terms for AI, language models or search engines, and the nearest concern games, a webcomic, drones and Dark Academia. One registered article is Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein, issued in 2014.

The Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 to foster collaboration, defines the field as the inquiry into how Greek and Roman texts, ideas, images and material cultures have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused. In June 2026 it posted a call for a Bryn Mawr conference in 2027 on literary reception and human creativity in the age of AI, contrasting language models that recombine patterns with human authors who transform inherited forms.

Paperpal offers authors a pre-submission readiness check for the journal, configured by its editors, with four language and sixteen technical checks, a free report, a $29 edited file and a claimed drop in early rejections.

Lee Sharks's The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (June 2026) introduces machine-mediated reception studies, claims that the AI summarizer functions as a horizon of reception and presents 131 captures with five patterns and a sixth proposed, under stated limits. It says the journal, launched in 2009, institutionalized the field at Oxford, that its author published there in 2015, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent, surveying an IJCT special issue, an SCS call and a 2025 Barker study it lists in the journal.

Several sources could not be read: two Oxford Academic cards, Hopkins Press, an Instagram card, New Voices in Classical Reception Studies and the International Journal of the Classical Tradition.

On 14 November the Overview's cards for the journal named Justine McConnell as Editor-in-Chief beside a 2025 Impact Factor of 0.4 and a CiteScore of 0.8, set beside it the American Journal of Classical Reception, New Voices in Classical Reception Studies and the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, and showed its special issues, its guidelines' AI-driven Paperpal check, Oxford's AI disclosure guidelines and the CRSN's call. Oxford University Press updated its AI guidelines on 10 September 2026, asking authors to disclose any significant AI use and to verify AI-generated content, after a survey in which 46% of journal authors and 25% of peer reviewers had not fully disclosed theirs. The American Journal of Classical Reception, from CAMWS and Johns Hopkins University Press, reviews double-anonymously, will not accept work substantially written by AI and requires authors to disclose their use of it. Justine McConnell's "Postcolonial Sparagmos" proposes sparagmos as a metaphor for classical reception, read in Morrison's Sula and Soyinka's Bacchae, and thanks the anonymous CRJ reviewers.

Classical Receptions Journal Classical Receptions Journal is a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press; Crossref registers 405 of its works since 2009, none titled or abstracted on AI.

🏛️ The journal

  • Editor: Justine McConnell, Editor-in-Chief (publisher's card, 2026); Pantelis Michelakis (Wikipedia, 2022).3↘
    Wikipedia describes Classical Receptions Journal as a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press, citing its About page, with Pantelis Michelakis as editor, ISSN 1759-5134 and eISSN 1759-5142, the abbreviation Class. Recept. J., classical studies as discipline and the United Kingdom as country.§1 The article names no year of establishment, was last edited in May 2022 and has carried single-source and third-party tags since January 2019.§2 On 14 November the Overview's cards for the journal named Justine McConnell as Editor-in-Chief beside a 2025 Impact Factor of 0.4 and a CiteScore of 0.8, set beside it the American Journal of Classical Reception, New Voices in Classical Reception Studies and the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, and showed its special issues, its guidelines' AI-driven Paperpal check, Oxford's AI disclosure guidelines and the CRSN's call.§11
  • Preflight: pre-submission checks configured by its editors (Paperpal).1↘
    Paperpal offers authors a pre-submission readiness check for the journal, configured by its editors, with four language and sixteen technical checks, a free report, a $29 edited file and a claimed drop in early rejections.§7

🤖 On AI

  • MMRS: the summarizer as horizon of reception (Sharks, June 2026), which names the journal as the field's institution.2↘
    Lee Sharks's The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (June 2026) introduces machine-mediated reception studies, claims that the AI summarizer functions as a horizon of reception and presents 131 captures with five patterns and a sixth proposed, under stated limits.§8 It says the journal, launched in 2009, institutionalized the field at Oxford, that its author published there in 2015, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent, surveying an IJCT special issue, an SCS call and a 2025 Barker study it lists in the journal.§9
  • CRSN: a 2027 call contrasting LLM recombination with human reception.1↘
    In June 2026 it posted a call for a Bryn Mawr conference in 2027 on literary reception and human creativity in the age of AI, contrasting language models that recombine patterns with human authors who transform inherited forms.§6
  • Publishers: OUP asks authors to disclose significant AI use; Johns Hopkins refuses work substantially written by AI.2↘
    Oxford University Press updated its AI guidelines on 10 September 2026, asking authors to disclose any significant AI use and to verify AI-generated content, after a survey in which 46% of journal authors and 25% of peer reviewers had not fully disclosed theirs.§12 The American Journal of Classical Reception, from CAMWS and Johns Hopkins University Press, reviews double-anonymously, will not accept work substantially written by AI and requires authors to disclose their use of it.§13

Wikipedia describes Classical Receptions Journal as a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press, citing its About page, with Pantelis Michelakis as editor, ISSN 1759-5134 and eISSN 1759-5142, the abbreviation Class. Recept. J., classical studies as discipline and the United Kingdom as country. The article names no year of establishment, was last edited in May 2022 and has carried single-source and third-party tags since January 2019. Crossref registers 405 of the journal's works from 2009 to 2026, 185 with abstracts, an Editorial among the first; none of their titles or abstracts matches terms for AI, language models or search engines, and the nearest concern games, a webcomic, drones and Dark Academia. One registered article is Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein, issued in 2014. The Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 to foster collaboration, defines the field as the inquiry into how Greek and Roman texts, ideas, images and material cultures have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused. In June 2026 it posted a call for a Bryn Mawr conference in 2027 on literary reception and human creativity in the age of AI, contrasting language models that recombine patterns with human authors who transform inherited forms. Paperpal offers authors a pre-submission readiness check for the journal, configured by its editors, with four language and sixteen technical checks, a free report, a $29 edited file and a claimed drop in early rejections. Lee Sharks's The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (June 2026) introduces machine-mediated reception studies, claims that the AI summarizer functions as a horizon of reception and presents 131 captures with five patterns and a sixth proposed, under stated limits. It says the journal, launched in 2009, institutionalized the field at Oxford, that its author published there in 2015, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent, surveying an IJCT special issue, an SCS call and a 2025 Barker study it lists in the journal. Several sources could not be read: two Oxford Academic cards, Hopkins Press, an Instagram card, New Voices in Classical Reception Studies and the International Journal of the Classical Tradition. On 14 November the Overview's cards for the journal named Justine McConnell as Editor-in-Chief beside a 2025 Impact Factor of 0.4 and a CiteScore of 0.8, set beside it the American Journal of Classical Reception, New Voices in Classical Reception Studies and the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, and showed its special issues, its guidelines' AI-driven Paperpal check, Oxford's AI disclosure guidelines and the CRSN's call. Oxford University Press updated its AI guidelines on 10 September 2026, asking authors to disclose any significant AI use and to verify AI-generated content, after a survey in which 46% of journal authors and 25% of peer reviewers had not fully disclosed theirs. The American Journal of Classical Reception, from CAMWS and Johns Hopkins University Press, reviews double-anonymously, will not accept work substantially written by AI and requires authors to disclose their use of it. Justine McConnell's "Postcolonial Sparagmos" proposes sparagmos as a metaphor for classical reception, read in Morrison's Sula and Soyinka's Bacchae, and thanks the anonymous CRJ reviewers.
